ER Visual Designer — System Design

A web-based tool for visually modelling relational database schemas for a selected database engine, validating them against that engine's rules, and generating ready-to-run DDL.

1. Purpose and scope

ER Visual Designer lets a user build a database schema on an interactive canvas instead of writing DDL by hand. The user picks a target engine (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle or SQLite), then creates tables and columns, sets keys and constraints, and links columns to form relationships. The tool continuously checks the model against the engine's rules, explains every problem with a suggested fix, and produces engine-specific DDL.

This document describes the target architecture for the full product. Delivery is phased; the phase plan and per-phase designs are in the companion ROADMAP document.

Change log — v1.1 (8 Nov 2026): visual direction decided (Sunrise Studio, §9.1), with design tokens, component styling, contrast check and responsive rules (§9.4–9.7). v1.0 (6 Nov 2026): first draft.

1.1 Goals

# Goal Measure of success
G1 Model tables, columns, data types, PKs, FKs, nullability and defaults visually Every column property is editable without writing SQL
G2 Interactive canvas for arranging tables and drawing relationships Drag tables, pan/zoom, drag column-to-column to create an FK
G3 Engine-aware validation Data types, naming rules and constraint rules checked per engine
G4 Actionable feedback Every issue has a location, a plain-language explanation and, where possible, a one-click fix
G5 Engine-specific DDL DDL that runs unmodified on the selected engine, in dependency-safe order
G6 Extensible engine support A new engine is added as a plug-in, not by changing core code

1.2 Non-goals (initial release)

  • Not a full SQL IDE: no arbitrary query editor or execution until the database-connectivity phases.
  • No views, stored procedures, triggers or partitions in the first model version (the model is designed so they can be added).
  • No real-time multi-user co-editing in the first release; the architecture leaves room for it (command log, see §7).

1.3 Terminology

Term Meaning
Model The engine-independent, serialisable description of a schema: tables, columns, constraints, plus layout
Dialect A plug-in describing one engine/version: types, naming rules, capabilities, DDL syntax
Logical type An engine-neutral type (e.g. integer, string(n), timestamp_tz) that maps to a physical type per dialect
Issue A validation result (error, warning or info) attached to a model element
Quick fix A model command attached to an issue that resolves it when applied
Command An undoable, serialisable change to the model (e.g. AddColumn, MoveTable)

2.2 Non-functional requirements

Category Requirement
Responsiveness Canvas interactions at 60 fps for 200 tables; usable up to 1,000 tables with viewport culling
Latency Validation results under 150 ms after an edit for a 200-table model (incremental, off the UI thread)
Layout Responsive from 360 px phones to 4K screens; panels collapse into drawers/bottom sheets below 900 px
Accessibility WCAG 2.2 AA: keyboard operation of canvas and panels, screen-reader labels, non-colour severity cues
Reliability No lost work: autosave every change (debounced) and crash-safe recovery from IndexedDB

Portability Model file format is versioned JSON with forward migrations
Extensibility Engines, validation rules and exporters are registered plug-ins

3. Architecture overview

The system is a TypeScript monorepo. Phases 1–5 run entirely in the browser with no backend: modelling, validation and DDL generation are pure functions over the model. Phases 6–8 add a backend service, because browsers cannot open database connections and credentials must stay server-side.

The core design principle is a single source of truth: one immutable model, changed only through commands. Canvas, inspector, problems panel and DDL view are all projections of that model.

3.1 Component diagram

Figure 1 — Component diagram. UI components never change state directly: they dispatch commands to the core and re-render from the model store. Validation and DDL generation run in workers and read all engine knowledge from the dialect registry. The backend appears only in Phase 6, behind the API client.

3.2 Component responsibilities

Component Responsibility Key interfaces
App shell & toolbar Layout of panels, engine selector, global actions, keyboard shortcuts, responsive breakpoints dispatches commands; reads view state
Explorer panel Searchable list of model tables (Model tab) and live database tree (Database tab, Phase 6) selectElement(), importTables()
Diagram canvas Renders table nodes and relationship edges; handles drag, pan, zoom, connect; viewport culling emits MoveTables, CreateForeignKey; reads model, issues, selection
Inspector Forms for the selected table/column/FK, with per-dialect type pickers and inline field errors dispatches Update* commands
Problems panel Grouped, sortable, filterable issue list; navigate-to-element; apply quick fix reads issue set; dispatches quick-fix commands
DDL viewer Live, syntax-highlighted DDL for whole model or selection; copy/export reads generator output
Command bus Validates and applies commands, records inverse commands for undo/redo, coalesces drags, publishes change events dispatch(cmd), undo(), redo()

Validation engine Runs rules incrementally on changed elements in a worker; returns issues with fixes validate(model, dialect, changedIds)
DDL generator Topologically orders tables, emits statements via dialect templates, formats output generate(model, dialect, options)
Dialect registry Loads dialect plug-ins; exposes types, naming rules, reserved words, capabilities, type mappings get(engine, version)
Persistence adapter Autosave to IndexedDB; open/save .erd.json; schema-version migrations save(), load(), migrate()

Backend services Connections, introspection, DML execution, Excel-to-DML, metrics (Phases 6–8) REST + WebSocket API (§10)

3.4 Package structure

er-visual-designer/
├── packages/
│   ├── model/          # Domain types, JSON schema, commands, migrations
│   ├── dialects/       # Dialect SPI + postgres, mysql, mssql, oracle, sqlite
│   ├── validation/     # Rule engine + rule catalogue
│   ├── ddl/            # DDL generator, formatter, diff (migrations)
│   ├── web/            # React SPA (canvas, panels, workers)
│   ├── server/         # Fastify API (Phase 6+)
│   └── introspect/     # Catalogue queries per engine (Phase 6+)
└── e2e/                # Playwright tests

model, dialects, validation and ddl are pure, framework-free libraries with no DOM access. They run unchanged in the browser, in workers, on the server and in a future CLI.

4. Domain model

4.1 Class diagram

Figure 2 — Domain model. Elements reference each other by stable ID, never by name, so renames never break references.

4.2 Key modelling decisions

  1. Stable IDs, not names. Tables, columns and relationships have UUIDs (ULIDs). FKs reference column IDs, so renaming a column updates every relationship and the DDL automatically.
  2. Layout is separate from the schema. Positions, colours and viewport are stored in Layout, so moving a table is not a schema change. It does not trigger validation or DDL regeneration.
  3. Physical type plus logical type. Every column stores the engine's physical type (e.g. numeric(12,2)) and its logical type (decimal(12,2)). The logical type makes engine conversion deterministic (see §5.3).
  4. Relationships are first-class. An FK is a Relationship with ordered column pairs, so composite FKs and cardinality (1:1, 1:N, optional/mandatory) come from one structure.
  5. Constraint names are optional. If none is given, the generator derives a deterministic name (pk_<table>, fk_<child>_<parent>, uq_<table>_<cols>) that respects the dialect's length limit, using a hash suffix when truncation is needed.

4.3 Serialised project format (.erd.json)

{
  "formatVersion": 1,
  "name": "shop_schema",
  "target": { "engine": "postgresql", "version": "16" },
  "model": {
    "tables": [{
      "id": "t_01HF...", "name": "orders", "schema": "public",
      "columns": [
        { "id": "c_01", "name": "id", "type": { "name": "bigint", "logical": "int64" },
          "nullable": false, "identity": { "kind": "always" } },
        { "id": "c_02", "name": "customer_id", "type": { "name": "bigint", "logical": "int64" }, "nullable": false },
        { "id": "c_03", "name": "status", "type": { "name": "varchar", "length": 20, "logical": "string" },
          "nullable": false, "default": { "kind": "literal", "value": "pending" } }
      ],
      "primaryKey": { "name": "pk_orders", "columnIds": ["c_01"] }
    }],
    "relationships": [{
      "id": "r_01", "name": "fk_orders_customer",
      "childTableId": "t_01HF...", "parentTableId": "t_01HE...",
      "columns": [{ "child": "c_02", "parent": "c_10" }],
      "onDelete": "restrict", "onUpdate": "no_action"
    }]
  },
  "layout": { "positions": { "t_01HF...": { "x": 420, "y": 80 } }, "viewport": { "x": 0, "y": 0, "zoom": 1 } }
}

The file is validated against a JSON Schema on load. A formatVersion change comes with a migration function, so old files always open.

5. Database engine dialects

5.1 Dialect plug-in interface

Each engine is a plug-in that implements a single interface. Validation, the inspector's type pickers and DDL generation get all engine-specific knowledge from this interface, so the core never contains if (engine === 'mysql') branches.

interface Dialect {
  id: EngineId;                         // 'postgresql' | 'mysql' | 'mssql' | 'oracle' | 'sqlite'
  displayName: string;
  versions: string[];                   // e.g. ['13','14','15','16','17']
  identifiers: {
    maxLength: number;                  // 63 PG, 64 MySQL, 128 SQL Server / Oracle 12.2+
    pattern: RegExp;                    // legal unquoted identifier
    caseFolding: 'lower' | 'upper' | 'preserve';
    quote(name: string): string;        // "x", `x`, [x]
    reservedWords: ReadonlySet<string>;
  };
  types: TypeDescriptor[];              // name, params (length/precision/scale ranges), category, aliases
  capabilities: {
    identity: 'generated' | 'auto_increment' | 'identity' | 'autoincrement';
    checkConstraints: boolean;
    deferrableConstraints: boolean;
    alterAddForeignKey: boolean;        // false for SQLite
    schemas: boolean;
    booleanType: boolean;
    onUpdateActions: RefAction[];
  };
  mapLogicalType(t: LogicalType): DataType | MappingWarning;
  toLogicalType(t: DataType): LogicalType;
  ddl: DdlTemplates;                    // createTable, column, pk, fk, unique, index, comment, drop
  rules?: ValidationRule[];             // engine-specific extra rules
}

5.2 Initial engine matrix

Capability PostgreSQL 13–17 MySQL 8.x SQL Server 2019+ Oracle 19c / 23ai SQLite 3.x
Max identifier length 63 bytes 64 chars 128 chars 128 bytes no limit
Unquoted case folding lower preserved (table names: OS-dependent) preserved (collation) upper preserved
Identifier quoting "name" `name` [name] "NAME" "name"
Auto-increment GENERATED … AS IDENTITY AUTO_INCREMENT IDENTITY(1,1) GENERATED … AS IDENTITY INTEGER PRIMARY KEY [AUTOINCREMENT]
Native boolean yes BOOLEAN = TINYINT(1) BIT 23ai only stored as integer
Add FK after create yes yes yes yes no — FKs must be inline
Schemas yes database = schema yes user = schema attached DBs only

The matrix is the starting point for the dialect plug-ins. Each value is backed by an automated test against the real engine (§12).

5.3 Logical type mapping

Converting a model between engines maps each physical type to its logical type, then to the target engine's physical type:

Logical PostgreSQL MySQL SQL Server Oracle SQLite
int32 integer INT INT NUMBER(10) INTEGER
int64 bigint BIGINT BIGINT NUMBER(19) INTEGER
decimal(p,s) numeric(p,s) DECIMAL(p,s) DECIMAL(p,s) NUMBER(p,s) NUMERIC
string(n) varchar(n) VARCHAR(n) NVARCHAR(n) VARCHAR2(n CHAR) TEXT
text text LONGTEXT NVARCHAR(MAX) CLOB TEXT
boolean boolean BOOLEAN BIT BOOLEAN (23ai) / NUMBER(1) INTEGER
timestamp_tz timestamptz TIMESTAMP ⚠ DATETIMEOFFSET TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE TEXT ⚠
uuid uuid BINARY(16) / CHAR(36) UNIQUEIDENTIFIER RAW(16) TEXT
json jsonb JSON NVARCHAR(MAX) ⚠ JSON (21c+) TEXT

⚠ marks lossy mappings. Each one produces a conversion warning that explains what is lost (for example, MySQL TIMESTAMP stores UTC and has a 2038 range limit).

6. Validation engine

6.1 Design

Validation is a set of small, independent rules. Each rule declares its scope (model, table, column or relationship) and the dialects it applies to. It is a pure function that returns zero or more issues.

interface ValidationRule {
  id: string;                         // e.g. 'E-TYP-001'
  scope: 'model' | 'table' | 'column' | 'relationship';
  appliesTo?: EngineId[];             // undefined = all engines
  defaultSeverity: 'error' | 'warning' | 'info';
  check(ctx: RuleContext): Issue[];
}

interface Issue {
  ruleId: string;
  severity: 'error' | 'warning' | 'info';
  target: { kind: 'table' | 'column' | 'relationship' | 'model'; id: Id; field?: string };
  message: string;                    // one line: what is wrong
  explanation: string;                // why it matters for this engine, with doc link
  fixes: QuickFix[];                  // each fix = label + Command[] (undoable)
}
  • Incremental. The command bus reports which element IDs changed. The engine re-runs only rules whose scope touches those elements, plus their FK neighbours. A full run happens on engine change or file load.
  • Off the main thread. Rules run in a dedicated Web Worker, so typing in the inspector never stutters.
  • Configurable. Users can change warning/info severities or suppress them per project (.erd.json → validation.overrides). Errors that would make the DDL fail cannot be suppressed.
  • Gating. Errors block DDL export (Phase 5) and apply-to-database (Phase 7). Warnings don't.

6.2 Rule catalogue (initial)

Rule ID Severity Checks Suggested fix
E-NAM-001 error Name is empty Generate name (table_1, column_1)
E-NAM-002 error Duplicate table name in schema / duplicate column name in table (respecting case-folding) Append suffix _2
E-NAM-003 error Identifier longer than the engine maximum Truncate with stable hash suffix
E-NAM-004 error / warn Reserved word used as identifier (error if the dialect forbids it even quoted, otherwise warning) Rename (e.g. order → orders) or quote always
W-NAM-005 warning Characters require quoting (spaces, mixed case on PG/Oracle) Convert to snake_case
E-TYP-001 error Data type not supported by engine/version Map via logical type
E-TYP-002 error Type parameter missing or out of range (e.g. VARCHAR without length on MySQL, DECIMAL(40,2) on SQL Server > 38) Clamp to the allowed range
E-DEF-001 error Default value not valid for the type (e.g. 'abc' on integer) Remove default / convert literal
E-DEF-002 error Default form not allowed for type on engine (e.g. literal default on MySQL TEXT/BLOB/JSON) Use expression default ('…') (MySQL 8.0.13+) or remove
E-PK-001 error Primary-key column is nullable Set NOT NULL
W-PK-002 warning Table has no primary key Add id identity column as PK
E-IDN-001 error Identity/auto-increment on non-integer type, or more than one per table (MySQL, SQL Server) Change type to bigint
E-FK-001 error FK column count differs from referenced key Open FK editor
E-FK-002 error FK column type is incompatible with the referenced column Change child type to match parent
E-FK-003 error Referenced columns are not a PK or unique constraint Add unique constraint on parent columns
W-FK-004 warning ON DELETE SET NULL on a NOT NULL column Make column nullable / change action
E-FK-005 error Referential action not supported (e.g. ON UPDATE on Oracle) Remove action
I-IDX-001 info FK columns have no supporting index (needed for join and delete performance) Add index
I-REL-001 info Circular FK dependency (handled by generator, but worth knowing) —
W-TBL-001 warning Table has no columns Add id column

6.3 Issue presentation

  • Canvas: a severity badge on the table header (highest severity wins) and a coloured underline on the offending column. The edge is dashed red for a broken relationship. Hovering shows the message.
  • Inspector: the offending field gets an inline error with the explanation and fix buttons.
  • Problems panel: grouped by table or by rule. It can be sorted by severity and filtered by text. Clicking an issue selects and centres the element. "Fix" applies the quick fix as one undoable command, and "Fix all of this kind" applies it as one batch.
  • Accessibility: severities use icon shape and text as well as colour (✖ error, ▲ warning, ● info).

7. State management, commands and undo/redo

All changes go through the command bus:

  1. A UI component dispatches a command, e.g. UpdateColumn { tableId, columnId, patch: { nullable: false } }.
  2. The bus checks structural invariants (target exists, IDs unique). It does not run engine rules; those produce issues, not rejections. This lets users work through intermediate invalid states.
  3. The bus applies the command with Immer, producing the next immutable model and an inverse command.
  4. The bus pushes { command, inverse } onto the history stack and emits a ModelChanged { changedIds } event.
  5. Subscribers react: the canvas re-renders affected nodes, the validator and DDL generator recompute (debounced 100 ms), and persistence autosaves (debounced 500 ms).

Coalescing. A drag emits many position updates. The canvas holds transient positions locally and dispatches one MoveTables command on drop, so undo returns the table to where it was before the drag. Continuous typing in one field is merged into a single history entry.

Transactions. Compound actions such as "create FK and create missing child column", or "apply all quick fixes", are wrapped in a Batch command, so they undo in one step.

Future collaboration. Commands are serialisable, so the same log can later be synchronised between users (e.g. through a CRDT/Yjs layer) without changing UI code.

8. DDL generation

8.1 Pipeline

Figure 3 — DDL generation pipeline.

  • Ordering. Tables are emitted in dependency order. FKs are emitted as separate ALTER TABLE statements after all tables by default, so cyclic references (e.g. employees.manager_id → employees.id, or A↔B) always work. An option inlines FKs when the graph has no cycles.
  • Quoting. Identifiers are quoted only when needed (reserved word, special characters, case-folding conflict), or always if the user chooses.
  • Source map. Each statement records the model element IDs it came from. Selecting a table highlights its DDL, and a DDL line can jump back to the canvas.
  • Options. Include DROP … IF EXISTS, wrap in a transaction (where DDL is transactional), include comments, target schema, statement terminator (; or GO).
  • Migrations (Phase 5). A diff of two model snapshots produces ALTER statements instead of CREATE statements.

8.2 Example output (same model, two engines)

-- PostgreSQL 16
CREATE TABLE "orders" (
  "id"          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,
  "customer_id" bigint NOT NULL,
  "status"      varchar(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
  "total"       numeric(12,2),
  CONSTRAINT "pk_orders" PRIMARY KEY ("id")
);
ALTER TABLE "orders" ADD CONSTRAINT "fk_orders_customer"
  FOREIGN KEY ("customer_id") REFERENCES "customers" ("id") ON DELETE RESTRICT;
CREATE INDEX "ix_orders_customer_id" ON "orders" ("customer_id");

-- SQL Server 2022
CREATE TABLE [orders] (
  [id]          BIGINT IDENTITY(1,1) NOT NULL,
  [customer_id] BIGINT NOT NULL,
  [status]      NVARCHAR(20) NOT NULL CONSTRAINT [df_orders_status] DEFAULT N'pending',
  [total]       DECIMAL(12,2) NULL,
  CONSTRAINT [pk_orders] PRIMARY KEY ([id])
);
GO
ALTER TABLE [orders] ADD CONSTRAINT [fk_orders_customer]
  FOREIGN KEY ([customer_id]) REFERENCES [customers] ([id]);
GO

9. User interface design

9.1 Chosen visual direction — Sunrise Studio

Decision (8 November 2026): of the three interactive mockups in mockups/ (A Aurora Glass, B Sunrise Studio, C Neon Flow), Option B — Sunrise Studio is the visual direction for the product. Options A and C are kept for reference only.

Sunrise Studio is a light, docked, IDE-style workspace. A warm coral → magenta → violet gradient marks the brand and the primary actions; everything else stays neutral, so the schema itself is the focus.

Figure 4 — Sunrise Studio (interactive mockup mockups/option-b-sunrise-studio.html). Desktop: gradient top bar with the database selector, palette and explorer (left), canvas, docked table editor (right), and the Problems/DDL panel (bottom). Phone: the explorer becomes a drawer, the editor a bottom sheet, and a floating "+" adds a table.

Why this direction

Criterion Sunrise Studio
Readability Highest contrast of the three options: dark text on white surfaces, and type names in monospace
Familiarity Docked layout like VS Code, DBeaver or DataGrip, so there is little to learn
Documentation Diagrams and screenshots print and paste into documents cleanly (light background)
Brand The gradient gives a distinctive identity without tinting the whole UI
Trade-off accepted A dark theme is a separate deliverable (derived from the same tokens, §9.4); it is not the default

Figure 5 — DDL tab: the database selector is repeated in the tab toolbar, with options (DROP IF EXISTS, quote all names), Generate / Copy / Download .sql, a warning banner while errors exist, and a dark syntax-highlighted code panel.

9.5 Component styling

Component Styling (Sunrise Studio)
Top bar Brand gradient with white text. Controls are translucent white (rgba(255,255,255,.16), 1 px rgba(255,255,255,.3) border). Generate DDL is the only solid white button, with pink text, so it stands out
Database selector Pill with a coloured dot for the engine (PostgreSQL blue, MySQL teal, SQL Server red, Oracle red, SQLite blue), shown in the top bar and repeated in the DDL tab
Palette items White cards with a gradient icon tile, title and hint. They lift 1 px with a pink glow on hover, and show a grab cursor. Clicking or tapping adds the item at the centre of the view (for touch)
Explorer Sections for Tables, Views and Relationships with count pills. The selected item uses the active gradient wash and pink text. A red or amber dot marks elements with errors or warnings
Table card 236 px wide with a gradient header (name and severity badge) and a white body. Each row shows a PK/FK marker, the name (with ? when nullable) and the monospace type. Connection dots appear on hover at both ends of every row. Rows with problems get a tinted background and a coloured left edge
View card Same card shape with the violet→blue header and a VIEW tag; the body shows the first lines of the SELECT
Relationship line 2 px violet curve with crow's foot (many) at the child and a double bar (one) at the parent. Errors show as dashed red; the selected line is thicker with a glow
Table editor Sticky header (gradient "TABLE" kicker and an editable title). Each column is a card: name, grouped type dropdown and size inputs on row 1; PK / NN / AI pill toggles (gradient when on), an FK pill, default value and delete on row 2. "+ Add column" is a dashed full-width button
Problems tab Filter pills (All / Errors / Warnings / Info with counts). Each row shows the severity icon, rule code (monospace), message, location and a ⚡ quick fix button. Clicking a row selects the element and pulses it
DDL tab Toolbar (database selector, options, Generate / Copy / .sql download) above the dark code panel with line numbers. An amber banner appears while the model has errors
Toast Dark pill at the bottom centre that confirms actions ("Linked …", "Fixed …"), with an undo hint for deletes

The production values keep the same hues and the same coral→magenta→violet direction, a little deeper. Severity is always shown with an icon and text (✖ ▲ ●) as well as colour.

9.7 Responsive behaviour

Width Layout
≥ 1,280 px Full layout: left 248 px, right 340 px, bottom 236 px, all toolbar actions visible
900–1,279 px Side panels narrow to 220 / 310 px; auto-layout moves into the overflow menu
< 900 px (tablet, phone) Single column (canvas above the bottom panel). ☰ opens the palette and explorer as a left drawer; selecting an element opens the editor as a bottom sheet (72 % height). Floating "+" adds a table. Toolbar shows the database selector, undo, the problems chip and DDL
< 480 px Brand name and info count hidden; the problems list shows only icon, message and fix

Touch: tap a palette item to add it, drag table headers to move tables, drag a column dot to link, and use pinch or the zoom buttons to zoom.

11. Backend and API (Phase 6+)

11.1 Deployment view

Figure 7 — Deployment view. The backend is stateless apart from connection pools, so it scales horizontally. It can be deployed on-premises next to the databases.

11.2 API surface (indicative)

Method Path Purpose
POST /api/connections Create connection (credentials stored encrypted)
POST /api/connections/{id}/test Test connectivity, return server version
GET /api/connections/{id}/catalog Schemas, tables, views with row estimates
POST /api/connections/{id}/introspect Return a model fragment for selected tables
GET /api/connections/{id}/tables/{t}/rows Paged, sorted, filtered rows (keyset pagination)
POST /api/connections/{id}/dml Execute a batch of parameterised DML in one transaction
POST /api/connections/{id}/ddl/apply Apply generated DDL (explicit opt-in, confirmation required)
WS /api/connections/{id}/metrics Stream metrics frames

11.3 Security

  • Credentials are sent once over TLS, encrypted at rest with envelope encryption (KMS), and never returned to the client.
  • Least privilege. Connections are read-only unless the user enables write mode for that connection. DML and DDL apply require write mode plus an explicit confirmation that shows the exact SQL.
  • No SQL injection. All DML is built server-side from structured requests with bound parameters. Identifiers are validated against the introspected catalogue and quoted by the dialect.
  • Auditing. Every write operation is logged with user, connection, statement hash and row counts.
  • Network. Optional allow-list of target hosts. Statement timeouts and row limits are enforced server-side.

12. Quality and testing strategy

Level What Tooling
Unit Commands and inverses (property test: apply then undo gives the original), each validation rule, type mappings, name generation Vitest + fast-check
Golden files DDL output per dialect for a corpus of models (cycles, composite keys, reserved words) Vitest snapshots
Engine conformance Generated DDL executed on real engines; introspecting it back must give an equivalent model (round-trip) Testcontainers: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle Free; SQLite in-process
Component Inspector forms, Problems panel, type pickers React Testing Library
End-to-end The sequences in §10, on desktop and mobile viewports Playwright (+ visual regression)
Performance 1,000-table model: render, drag, validate, generate budgets Playwright traces, benchmark CI job
Accessibility Keyboard-only flows, axe checks axe-core, manual screen-reader passes

13. Risks and open questions

Risk / question Impact Mitigation / proposal
Engine rules differ across versions (e.g. Oracle BOOLEAN only in 23ai) Wrong validation results Dialects are versioned. Rules declare minVersion/maxVersion, backed by conformance tests
Canvas performance on very large schemas Poor user experience Viewport culling, simplified level-of-detail rendering when zoomed out, subject-area views
Reverse-engineering edge cases (computed columns, domains, custom types) Incomplete import Import unsupported objects as "opaque" columns with a warning, never drop them silently
Live DML against production databases Data loss Read-only default, transaction plus preview, confirmation, audit log, optional "non-production only" flag
Open: hosted SaaS, on-premises, or both? Backend design, auth Proposal: build stateless and container-first so both are possible; decide before Phase 6
Open: project storage — local files only or server-side projects with sharing? Collaboration features Proposal: local-first in Phases 1–5; server projects optional from Phase 6
Open: which engine versions are "tier 1" at launch? Test matrix size Proposal: PostgreSQL 16/17, MySQL 8.4, SQL Server 2022, Oracle 23ai, SQLite 3.4x
